title: The history of the quartz watch
tagline: 140 years from a squeezed crystal in a Paris lab to a watch that drifts by one second a year.
intro: In 1880 two brothers in Paris found that some crystals make electricity when you squeeze them. Forty years later, engineers learned to make a sliver of quartz ring at one steady note, and by 1927 that note was running a clock the size of a room. Then came the hard part: shrinking the crystal, the counting circuit and the motor until they fitted on a wrist. Swiss and Japanese teams raced to do it in the 1960s, and the watch that followed changed who made the world's watches, from Switzerland to Japan to India.

eras.name: A spark from a squeezed crystal
eras.summary: Scientists find that quartz turns pressure into electricity, and electricity into movement. A war turns the lab trick into a real machine.

eras.name: Quartz keeps time in the lab
eras.summary: Radio engineers make quartz ring at one exact note. The note runs clocks so steady that they catch the Earth itself running fast and slow.

eras.name: The race to the wrist
eras.summary: Batteries, tuning forks and tiny chips arrive. Teams in Switzerland and Japan race to squeeze a quartz clock into a wristwatch.

eras.name: The quartz flood
eras.summary: Quartz watches get small, cheap and very accurate. Old watch companies struggle, and new ones appear from Japan to India.

eras.name: Chasing the last second
eras.summary: Quartz is everywhere, so makers find new tricks: power from your wrist and from light, time by radio, and crystals good to one second a year.

events.title: Squeeze a crystal, get electricity
events.text: Two brothers, Pierre and Jacques Curie, pressed on crystals of quartz, tourmaline, topaz, cane sugar and Rochelle salt. An electric charge appeared on the faces. In 1881 Gabriel Lippmann worked out from the maths that the reverse must also be true, and the brothers quickly showed it: a voltage makes the crystal change shape.
events.why: This two-way link between pushing and electricity, called piezoelectricity, is what lets a watch make its quartz crystal vibrate and then listen to it.

events.title: Quartz goes to war under the sea
events.text: During the First World War, Paul Langevin needed a way to find submarines. In February 1917 he used a slice of quartz to pick up sound, and by April he was using quartz to send sound out too. Sea tests at Toulon in 1918 found submerged submarines up to 1,300 metres away.
events.why: It was the first real job for piezoelectric quartz, and it got engineers thinking about what else a vibrating crystal could do.

events.title: A crystal that holds one note
events.text: Walter Cady found that a bar of quartz in an electric circuit rings at one very exact frequency. On 28 December 1921 he described the first quartz oscillator circuit, using a bar 39 mm long that vibrated about 70,000 times a second. In 1923 George Pierce at Harvard published a simpler circuit, and almost every quartz clock chip today uses a version of it.
events.why: A circuit could now be locked to the steady ringing of a crystal, which is the heart of every quartz watch.

events.title: The first quartz clock
events.where: Bell Telephone Laboratories, New York, USA
events.text: Warren Marrison, a Canadian engineer, and Joseph Horton used a block of quartz vibrating 50,000 times a second. A divider circuit counted the vibrations down until they were slow enough to turn a small motor and move clock hands. Marrison only wanted to measure radio frequencies, but he had built a clock. He made a better one in 1928.
events.why: It showed the full recipe a quartz watch still follows: crystal, divider, motor, hands.

events.title: Quartz catches the Earth running unevenly
events.who: Adolf Scheibe and Udo Adelsberger, and Nicolas Stoyko
events.text: Adolf Scheibe and Udo Adelsberger ran quartz clocks at Germany's national standards lab in Berlin. Between 1935 and 1937 they, and Nicolas Stoyko in Paris, showed that the Earth spins a little faster and slower with the seasons. The length of a day changes by about a thousandth of a second through the year.
events.why: For the first time a human-made clock kept better time than the spinning planet, and by the 1940s time labs around the world had swapped pendulums for quartz.

events.title: A motor that moves one tick at a time
events.text: French engineer Marius Lavet filed a patent for a very simple electric motor. Each short pulse of current flips a tiny magnet half a turn, then it waits for the next pulse. It needs very little power.
events.why: Shrunk down, the Lavet motor is what moves the second hand of almost every quartz watch and clock with hands.

events.title: The watch that hums
events.text: Watches had always used a swinging balance wheel. Hamilton kept the wheel but swapped the spring for a battery in its Electric 500, announced on 3 January 1957. Then Bulova's Accutron, designed by Swiss-born engineer Max Hetzel, dropped the balance wheel completely. A tiny tuning fork hummed 360 times a second, and Bulova promised it would stay within one minute a month.
events.why: It proved a faster, steadier vibration makes a better watch, and it pushed Swiss and Japanese makers to try quartz, which vibrates far faster still.

events.title: India starts making wristwatches
events.text: HMT signed a deal with Citizen of Japan in March 1960 to learn how to make watches. On 28 July 1961 Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru unveiled the first batch of 800 hand-wound watches in Bangalore. The Janata model later became a favourite gift for passing exams.
events.why: It gave India its own watch industry, built on mechanical watches, just before quartz changed everything.

events.title: A chip that sips power
events.text: Frank Wanlass and Chih-Tang Sah showed a new way to build logic circuits, pairing two opposite kinds of transistor. The circuit used almost no power while it sat waiting. Wanlass filed the patent on 18 June 1963. Today it is called CMOS.
events.why: A watch chip must count thousands of vibrations every second for years on one tiny battery, and CMOS made that possible.

events.title: A quartz clock you can carry to the Olympics
events.text: Seiko's engineers had begun their quartz project in 1959. For the 1964 Tokyo Olympics they built the Crystal Chronometer QC-951, a portable quartz clock that ran on batteries and was off by only 0.2 seconds a day. Seiko brought 1,278 timing instruments to the Games.
events.why: Quartz had shrunk from a room of equipment to a box you could carry, and the next step was the wrist.

events.title: Beta 1: the first quartz wristwatch prototype
events.text: Swiss watch companies had set up a shared lab, the CEH, in 1962. Its quartz wristwatch project began in November 1965. In July 1967 a small crew assembled Beta 1, with its own chip made on Switzerland's first chip pilot line. Armin Frei, one of its engineers, says it was very probably the first quartz wristwatch anywhere. Seiko built its own prototype the same year.
events.why: It proved a quartz clock could fit on a wrist, though no one could buy one yet.

events.title: Quartz sweeps the Neuchâtel trials
events.text: Every year the Neuchâtel Observatory tested the world's most accurate watches. In 1967 quartz wristwatches entered for the first time. CEH prototypes took all of the top ten places, with a best score of 0.152. Seiko's five quartz prototypes placed from 11th, with a best score of 0.301. Lower is better.
events.why: Both teams beat anything a mechanical wristwatch had ever scored, so the race to sell one was on.

events.title: The Seiko Quartz Astron goes on sale
events.who: Tsuneya Nakamura's team at Suwa Seikosha
events.text: After ten years of work, Seiko put the first quartz wristwatch in the shops on Christmas Day 1969. The gold Astron 35SQ cost 450,000 yen, about the price of a car. Its crystal vibrated 8,192 times a second and it was rated to within 5 seconds a month. One hundred were sold in the first week.
events.why: The Swiss built the first prototype, but Seiko was first to sell a quartz watch to the public. The IEEE made it a Milestone in 2004.

events.title: Beta 21: the Swiss answer
events.who: CEH and a group of Swiss watch companies
events.text: Less than four months after the Astron, the first Swiss quartz watches arrived. The Beta 21 movement, grown from the CEH prototypes, was shared by a group of Swiss brands and shown at the 1970 Basel Fair. The first 1,000 were ready on 10 April 1970.
events.why: Switzerland had the technology too, but the watches were costly and few, and Japan moved faster to make quartz cheap.

events.title: Tuning forks printed like chips
events.text: Early watch crystals were cut and tuned one at a time. In the late 1960s Juergen Staudte, a German-born physicist in California, used the photo-printing methods of chip makers to etch many tiny quartz tuning forks from one thin wafer. He started a company, Statek, to make them.
events.why: Batch-made tuning-fork crystals were small and cheap, and they are still the kind inside nearly every quartz watch.

events.title: The recipe settles: 32,768 and CMOS
events.text: In 1971 the Swiss maker Girard-Perregaux brought out its Caliber 350 with a crystal vibrating 32,768 times a second. The same year Seiko began mass production of a CMOS watch chip with its 38SQW. Nearly all quartz watches since have used both ideas.
events.why: 32,768 is 2 multiplied by itself 15 times, so a simple chip can halve it 15 times to get exactly one tick a second.

events.title: Twelve seconds a year
events.text: Omega's Marine Chronometer wristwatch used a crystal vibrating about 2.4 million times a second, far faster than normal. It was rated to 12 seconds a year, which is one second a month.
events.why: It showed that a faster crystal makes a steadier watch, an idea makers came back to decades later.

events.title: The quartz crisis
events.text: Cheap, accurate quartz watches from Japan and elsewhere poured into shops. Many Swiss makers had bet on mechanical watches and could not keep up. Between 1970 and 1983 the number of Swiss watchmaking companies fell from 1,600 to 600. Jobs fell from about 90,000 in 1970 to 28,000 by 1988.
events.why: A better way to keep time put two thirds of an industry's workers out of a job, and forced Switzerland to reinvent its watches.

events.title: A watch that runs on light
events.text: Early quartz watches ate through batteries quickly. Citizen's Crystron Solar Cell put solar cells on the dial to top up its battery. Citizen describes it as the world's first light-powered quartz watch with hands.
events.why: It began the idea of a quartz watch that never needs a new battery.

events.title: Two crystals beat the weather
events.text: A quartz crystal runs a little fast or slow as it warms and cools. Seiko's Twin Quartz watches carried a second crystal that worked as a thermometer, so the watch could correct itself. The Grand Twin Quartz was rated to 10 seconds a year, and the Superior Twin Quartz to 5.
events.why: Correcting for temperature is still the main way to make a quartz watch more accurate.

events.title: Delirium: thinner than two millimetres
events.text: Japanese makers were winning a race to build the thinnest watch. The Swiss replied with the Delirium, just 1.98 mm thick, sold by Concord, Eterna and Longines. The trick was to build the parts straight onto the back of the case. A later version was 0.98 mm thick and too thin to wear.
events.why: Building the movement into the case was the idea that led to the Swatch.

events.title: Swatch: 51 parts and a plastic case
events.who: Ernst Thomke, Elmar Mock and Jacques Müller
events.text: Engineers Elmar Mock and Jacques Müller designed a plastic quartz watch with only 51 parts, put together by machines. The first twelve models were shown in Zürich on 1 March 1983, at prices under 50 Swiss francs. Nicolas Hayek later led the company that became the Swatch Group.
events.why: A cheap, cheerful, Swiss-made quartz watch helped pull the Swiss industry out of its crisis.

events.title: Titan brings quartz to India
events.text: Titan was set up in 1984 by the Tata Group and the Tamil Nadu state development corporation, TIDCO. Its first watches went on sale in 1987, all quartz, priced from 350 to 900 rupees. HMT had sold quartz watches earlier, but it moved slowly. Titan's hundreds of modern designs won over buyers.
events.why: India's watches changed from wind-up to quartz within a few years, and Titan grew into one of the world's biggest watchmakers.

events.title: A quartz watch you power by moving
events.text: Seiko's A.G.S. watch had a swinging weight, like a self-winding mechanical watch. Instead of winding a spring, the weight spun a tiny generator that made electricity for the quartz circuit. Seiko later renamed it Kinetic.
events.why: It joined the oldest trick in self-winding watches to the accuracy of quartz.

events.title: A watch that listens to an atomic clock
events.text: The Junghans Mega 1 was the first radio-controlled wristwatch. An aerial hidden in the strap picked up the DCF77 time signal sent from Mainflingen in Germany, and the watch set itself. The first model had a digital display. A version with hands followed in 1991.
events.why: A quartz watch no longer had to be perfect on its own, because it could check itself against an atomic clock every day.

events.title: Light power and five seconds a year
events.text: In 1995 Citizen began selling its light-powered watches under the name Eco-Drive, first in Asia, Latin America and Europe. A solar cell behind the dial charges a rechargeable battery. The same year it launched a top line called The Citizen, with early quartz models rated to 5 seconds a year.
events.why: Solar quartz became an everyday thing, and very high accuracy became something you could buy off the shelf.

events.title: Spring Drive: a spring with a quartz brain
events.text: Yoshikazu Akahane had the idea in 1977: power a watch with a wound spring, but let a quartz crystal control its speed. It took more than 600 prototypes. The watch has no battery and its second hand glides smoothly. It is rated to one second a day.
events.why: It showed quartz is a way of keeping time, not just a kind of battery watch.

events.title: Titan Edge: 3.5 mm thin
events.who: B. G. Dwarakanath and the Titan team
events.text: In 1997 Titan engineers B. G. Dwarakanath and Subramanya Bhat proposed an ultra-slim quartz movement. It was working by 2000. The Titan Edge was launched in May 2002. The watch is 3.5 mm thick and its movement, battery included, is 1.15 mm. Titan called it the slimmest watch in the world.
events.why: A young Indian watchmaker designed and built a movement that matched the best in Switzerland and Japan.

events.title: Eight times faster
events.text: Bulova's Precisionist used a crystal vibrating 262,144 times a second, eight times the usual 32,768. Bulova claimed it was accurate to 10 seconds a year. Its second hand sweeps smoothly instead of ticking.
events.why: It brought the faster-crystal idea back in a watch ordinary buyers could afford.

events.title: One second a year
events.text: Citizen's Caliber 0100 is rated to within one second a year, with no help from radio or satellite signals. It uses a different cut of quartz that vibrates 8,388,608 times a second, more than 250 times faster than a tuning-fork crystal. It runs on light. Citizen announced three limited models on 20 March 2019, 800 watches in all.
events.why: It is about 60 times better than the first Astron, and about as good as a watch on its own has ever been.

series.title: How far a landmark watch could drift in a year
series.caption: Each point is the maker's own rated accuracy, turned into seconds of error per year. In sixty years the drift shrank about 700 times.

facts: 32,768 is 2 multiplied by itself 15 times. A watch chip cuts the crystal's beat in half 15 times and ends up with exactly one pulse a second.
When Paul Langevin first tried quartz as an underwater microphone in 1917, he laid a watch on the crystal and heard it tick through a loudspeaker.
The first Seiko Quartz Astron cost 450,000 yen, about as much as a car. One hundred were sold in a week.
In the 1930s quartz clocks became steadier than the spinning Earth, and showed that the length of a day changes with the seasons.
A normal quartz watch gains or loses about 15 seconds a month, mostly because of temperature. The best one made drifts by one second a year.
